clinicalPearls: A focal variant of the stiff person spectrum in which rigidity and painful spasms are largely confined to one limb, most often a distal leg or foot, sometimes with fixed dystonic posturing such as an equinovarus deformity.
Continuous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles produces board-like rigidity, with spontaneous and stimulus-sensitive painful spasms.
Electromyography shows continuous motor unit activity in the affected limb that persists at rest and is abolished by benzodiazepines, sleep or peripheral nerve block.
Compared with classic axial stiff person syndrome, glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies are less consistently present; some cases carry glycine receptor or amphiphysin (paraneoplastic) antibodies.
Sphincter disturbance, brainstem signs or spread to other limbs and axial muscles may develop, and there can be overlap with progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus.
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by electromyography, antibody testing and a therapeutic response to GABAergic agents such as benzodiazepines or baclofen.
Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange, rituximab) is used, but response is often less complete than in classic disease and fixed contractures may result.
Where paraneoplastic antibodies such as amphiphysin are found, an underlying malignancy (classically breast) should be sought.
reference.pathophysiology: Stiff limb syndrome is an autoimmune disorder of impaired inhibitory neurotransmission within the spinal cord. Loss of GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition, driven by antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (the enzyme synthesising GABA), the glycine receptor, or the presynaptic protein amphiphysin, releases spinal motor circuits from descending and segmental control. The result is continuous involuntary co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles that produces sustained rigidity with superimposed spasms, frequently triggered by touch, movement, noise or emotion. In the focal variant the process is regionally restricted, most often to a lower limb, although it can spread proximally or to the axial and brainstem musculature. Paraneoplastic cases, typically amphiphysin-associated, reflect an immune response directed at tumour antigens that are shared with neural tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
Focal or fixed dystonia (organic or functional)
Spinal cord pathology (compressive myelopathy or tumour) causing focal rigidity
additionalInvestigations: Needle electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity abolished by benzodiazepines
Serum and cerebrospinal fluid glutamic acid decarboxylase, glycine receptor and amphiphysin antibodies
MRI of the spine and brain to exclude structural mimics
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including oligoclonal bands and cell count
Screening for associated autoimmune disease such as thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes
Malignancy screening (including breast imaging) where paraneoplastic antibodies are present
Documented therapeutic response to a GABAergic agent as supportive evidence
redFlags: Rapid spread with truncal or respiratory muscle involvement or brainstem signs, raising concern for progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity
Features suggesting occult malignancy such as weight loss or a breast mass
Sudden violent spasms causing falls, fractures or joint dislocation
Development of fixed contractures threatening mobility
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; symptomatic and immunotherapy can reduce spasms and rigidity, but the limb variant often responds less completely than classic disease and may leave fixed deformity. Prognosis in paraneoplastic cases depends on the underlying tumour.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as functional or psychogenic dystonia and delaying immunotherapy.
Assuming glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies must be present, when their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
Missing a paraneoplastic cause by omitting amphiphysin testing and malignancy screening.
Overlooking evolution into progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity, with its life-threatening brainstem and autonomic involvement.
Abruptly withdrawing benzodiazepines or baclofen and precipitating severe rebound spasms.
references: Stiff person spectrum disorder clinical reviews
management: GABAergic symptomatic therapy with benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) and/or baclofen to reduce rigidity and painful spasms
Immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab in refractory disease
Botulinum toxin injection for focal dystonic posturing and fixed deformity such as equinovarus
Physiotherapy and regular stretching to preserve range of movement and prevent contractures
Investigate for and treat any underlying tumour in amphiphysin-associated paraneoplastic cases
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes and thyroid disorders
Neurology referral with monitoring for spread to axial and brainstem muscles or overlap with progressive encephalomyelitis
